title: The same word
hook: two verses sharing a word may share a law

segments.voice: Yesterday, kal vachomer, and your line: if this, then surely that. Light to heavy, with a stop on the lever. Did you carry a small kindness home? Today, a second tool, and this one runs on words. Day one thousand ninety-six.

Two people who've never met mention the same small town, and suddenly they're talking like cousins. A shared word can do that: it builds a bridge between two places that seemed to have nothing to do with each other. The rabbis noticed the Torah can do it too. A verse about a burial plot bought from a stranger, and a verse about a man marrying a woman, sit books apart. They share one ordinary verb. And on that one verb, the Talmud builds a bridge strong enough to carry a law. Today's word is the bridge.
screen: `THE SAME SMALL TOWN.` → `A BURIAL PLOT, A MARRIAGE.` → `ONE VERB BETWEEN THEM.`

segments.voice: Gezerah shavah. The rule that when two verses share a word, they may share a law. What's clear in one place can be carried to the other. Here's the bridge from the hook. The Mishnah, at the opening of tractate Kiddushin, lists the ways a marriage can begin, and one of them is with money. The Gemara asks: how do we know money works? The answer is a gezerah shavah on the word take. In Deuteronomy, the Torah speaks of a man who takes a wife. In Genesis, Abraham is buying a cave to bury Sarah, and he says to Ephron, the owner of the field, that he'll give the money for it: take it from me. Take there, take here. In Genesis, taking happens with money. So in Deuteronomy, taking a wife can happen with money too. That's the move, and notice what it isn't. It isn't a pun, and it isn't a vibe. The Talmud treats it as a rule with serious limits. The big one: the Talmud says a person may not make up a gezerah shavah on their own. It has to come down from teachers who received it. Without that limit, anyone could link any two verses that share a common word, and make the Torah say almost anything. So the bridge is real, but you don't get to build new ones on a whim. You walk the ones that were handed to you. And under the rule sits a classical belief: that the Torah's words are chosen so carefully that the same word in two places can carry meaning across. Same word, same law.
screen: `TWO VERSES, ONE WORD.` · `TAKE: A FIELD AND A MARRIAGE.` · `NOT A PUN: A RULE.` · `RECEIVED, NOT MADE UP.` · then, large: `SAME WORD, SAME LAW.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to link two ideas. Breathe out once, a little longer than usual. Choose one word that matters to you: home, maybe, or rest, or enough. Now find two places in your life where that word lives. Where is home in your body? Where is home in a person? Hold both places at once, and let the word be the bridge between them. Does what's true of one say something about the other? Don't force it. Just walk across, slowly, a few times. The bell holds the time.
Gezerah shavah. When two verses share a word, they may share a law, but only along bridges a person received from teachers. Today's word.
Your line: same word, same law. Today, listen for one word you hear twice in different places, from two people or two signs, and ask what the two might teach each other. Day one thousand ninety-six.

howItsDone: Talmud students learn each gezerah shavah as a link handed down by earlier teachers, tracing the shared word back to both verses rather than inventing new links of their own.

original.note: Hebrew: the rule that links two verses through a shared word.

trapdoor: what you thought: matching words to get the answer you wanted.
what it means: a received bridge between two verses through one shared word, so a law clear in one applies to the other.
what a scholar hears: Kiddushin 2a's kicha-kicha from the field of Ephron, and the principle that one does not derive a gezerah shavah on one's own.

notes: Kiddushin 2a's derivation (kicha kicha mi-sedeh Efron) is paraphrased; please confirm it is fair to say 'in Genesis, taking happens with money'.
Genesis 23:13 and Deuteronomy 24:1 are paraphrased, not quoted; the voice's 'take it from me' is a paraphrase in plain words.
The principle that a person does not derive a gezerah shavah on his own (ein adam dan gezerah shavah me-atzmo) is cited to Pesachim 66a and Niddah 19b; please confirm the folios.

'The Torah's words are chosen so carefully that the same word in two places is never just an accident' is offered as the belief underlying the rule; please confirm it is fair across Orthodox and non-Orthodox readings, or soften to 'a classical belief'.
